title: Breakfast at Tiffany's
tagline: Grace in every frame, humanity in every cause.

scenes.text: Hollywood, 1953. A twenty-four year old Belgian actress arrives from the London stage. Her face is unlike any Hollywood had seen — all cheekbones and enormous dark eyes. Within a year she will win an Oscar, a Tony, and change what beauty means to an entire generation.

scenes.speaker: Audrey Hepburn
scenes.text: I was a war child. I was hungry — truly hungry, as a child in occupied Netherlands. That changes you. I cannot look at abundance without thinking of those who have none. Which is why, in the end, UNICEF matters more to me than cinema.

challenge.instruction: Paramount needs clothes for Sabrina, and Audrey goes to Paris to find a young couturier called Hubert de Givenchy. Share the work across the atelier so the wardrobe is ready before the cameras roll.
challenge.fact: Sabrina (1954) won the Academy Award for costume design, but the Oscar went to the studio designer Edith Head, and Givenchy's name was left off the credits. Hepburn made sure he was credited on her later films.

scenes.text: In her final years, Hepburn served as a UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador, traveling to Somalia, Ethiopia, Sudan, and Bangladesh — places far from Hollywood's lights. She called her humanitarian work her greatest role.

challenge.instruction: As UNICEF's Goodwill Ambassador, Audrey goes where the cameras rarely go. Plan her missions from home in Switzerland to Ethiopia, then Bangladesh, and at last to Somalia.
challenge.fact: Hepburn became a UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador in 1988 for a token salary of one dollar a year. As a starving child in Holland in 1945 she had been fed by the Allied relief agencies that were the forerunners of UNICEF.

scenes.speaker: Audrey Hepburn
scenes.text: I believe in pink. I believe that laughing is the best calorie burner. I believe in kissing, kissing a lot. I believe in being strong when everything seems to be going wrong. I believe that happy girls are the prettiest girls.

challenge.instruction: Dawn on Fifth Avenue, a black dress and a pastry at Tiffany's window — the scene that made Audrey an icon. Fit the pieces together until the opening of Breakfast at Tiffany's is whole.
challenge.fact: 'Moon River' won the 1962 Academy Award for Best Original Song. When a Paramount executive suggested cutting it, Hepburn reportedly said: 'Over my dead body!' Henry Mancini wrote the melody to suit her small vocal range.

scenes.text: Audrey's path from wartime Netherlands to Hollywood stardom was a journey through chaos and reinvention. Navigate her story to reach the iconic moment...

challenge.instruction: Arnhem, 1944 — long before Hollywood. Help teenage Audrey slip through the occupied streets for the resistance, past the patrols and the mines, and home again.
challenge.fact: Hepburn spent the war in the Netherlands. In 1942 the occupiers executed her uncle, and her half-brother was sent to a labour camp in Germany. In the Hunger Winter of 1944–45 she lived on scraps, including flour made from tulip bulbs.

challenge.instruction: In Funny Face Audrey sweeps down the Louvre's grand staircase beneath the Winged Victory. Hang the treasures so every gallery tells one story, then open the doors.
challenge.fact: In Funny Face (1957) Hepburn runs down the Daru staircase of the Louvre past the Winged Victory of Samothrace, a red chiffon scarf streaming behind her, while Fred Astaire's photographer shouts 'Take the picture!'

challenge.instruction: Years after Audrey's death, her black Givenchy gown goes under the hammer to build schools for poor children in India. Win the starred lots for the cause.
challenge.fact: In December 2006 the black Givenchy gown from Breakfast at Tiffany's sold at Christie's in London for £467,200, several times its estimate. The money went to City of Joy Aid, Dominique Lapierre's charity, to build schools for children in India.

scenes.speaker: Audrey Hepburn
scenes.text: Mother Teresa and Joël Robuchon are still in the rival's hand; they will come to the board one by one. Follow them, start the Art Critique where they stand, and fight with Kill mode on. A player with no Great People left is out of the game.

challenge.instruction: Fight lesson 7 · Conquest. Deploy, move to wherever the rival stands, start the Art Critique there, and attack with Kill mode on until the rival has no Great People left.
challenge.fact: With Kill mode on, a beaten card is discarded instead of returning to hand. A player with no Great People left, in hand or on the board, is out, and the last player standing wins. A kill won in a Great Person's own stat also counts towards their achievement.
